narrative:
The model determined that you have a 73.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your academic performance in the later years of college, your LSAT score, and your undergraduate grades. Your position in the bottom decile of your class for Year 3 was the single strongest reason the model predicted failure; it pulled the outcome strongly toward not passing. Your LSAT score of 26, which sits far below the average of 37 among accepted students, also pushed the prediction noticeably toward failure. Although your undergraduate GPA of 2.9 was slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and therefore worked against you, its influence was smaller than the first two factors and actually pulled the prediction slightly back toward passing.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score and strengthening your academic record in any remaining coursework or through targeted bar-preparation programs. Retaking the LSAT with a higher score would be the single most helpful step you can take next. (218 words)
